newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin meets Chirac on French cabinet list.
newsitem.headline: Jospin meets Chirac on French cabinet list.

text.p: New French Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin met President Jacques Chirac on Wednesday to offer a broad-left cabinet list including two Communist ministers, as Chirac's defeated Gaullist party wallowed in recrimination.

Jospin arrived at the Elysee palace after completing talks with the Communist party, the ecologist Greens and the anti-Maastricht Citizens' Movement which were all expected to join a government dominated by his Socialist party.

Communist leader Robert Hue confirmed that the Communists would take part in the cabinet for the first time since they walked out on the Socialists in 1984. Grassroots members voted overwhelmingly in favour of participating.

He did not say what, if any, assurances he had obtained on Communist demands. These include a higher minimum wage, a cut in value-added tax and speedy implementation of promises to create 700,000 youth jobs and cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 to attack record 12.8 percent unemployment.
But he told reporters: "The Communist party is fully aware of the scale of efforts that need to be accomplished and of the role it will play along with the labour and citizens' movement."
Jospin received a warm letter of congratulations from U.S. President Bill Clinton and talked with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, France's main European ally, aides said.

Chirac's own authority came under fire on the right, with a growing chorus of Gaullists demanding the immediate removal of defeated ex-prime minister Alain Juppe as leader of his RPR party and the heads of several of the president's closest aides.
Before finalising his list of 17 ministers, expected to include seven women and one representative each of the Greens party and Citizens' Movement, Jospin reorganised his own party on Wednesday.
Former prime minister Laurent Fabius was nominated for president of the new National Assembly, in which the combined left will have a 62-seat majority over the centre-right.

Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande will take over as acting party leader while Jospin, the first secretary, serves as premier and Jean-Marc Ayrault, mayor of the western city of Nantes, will be the Socialists' parliamentary floor leader.

Fabius, who was previously parliamentary speaker from 1988 to 1992, defeated former environment minister Segolene Royal by 40 votes to five in a ballot for the post, known in French politics as "the perch".
The appointments mean that Royal is likely to join Jospin's government along with Daniel Vaillant, the party's number two, a probable interior minister, party sources said.
Jospin, 59, faces the first major test of "cohabitation" power-sharing with Chirac over the cabinet. The constitution gives the president a veto over appointees.
The new prime minister maintained strict secrecy about his "Pink-Green-Red" cabinet list, perhaps to ensure Chirac had no objections to the key ministers before announcing them.
Socialist sources said former industry minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn, regarded by financial markets as a safe pair of hands, would be finance minister.

Press reports said Jospin could name former European affairs minister Elisabeth Guigou as France's first woman foreign minister, and Hubert Vedrine, a former chief aide to late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand, as defence minister.
But other candidates mentioned for both posts included former justice minister Henri Nallet and former Mitterrand aide and transport minister Jean-Louis Bianco.
For the Communists, Jean-Claude Gayssot was expected to be transport minister and Marie George Buffet to get the youth and sports portfolio, party officials said.

Guigou, 50, a cool technocrat who entered politics as an adviser to Mitterrand, was elected to the National Assembly for the first time on Sunday. She is also a member of the European Parliament, closely involved in negotiations on the current reform of European Union institutions.

Vedrine, 49, played a key role in both previous periods of left-right power-sharing. He was diplomatic adviser and spokesman for Mitterrand before becoming secretary-general of the president's office. Aides to Chirac say he has "a sense of the state" and the president respects him.
Out of office, Juppe struggled to cling to his job as Gaullist party boss as erstwhile allies sharpened their knives.
Pierre Mazeaud, a veteran Gaullist parliamentarian, blamed Juppe and top aides to Chirac for convincing him to call a snap election which backfired disastrously.
"(Chirac) must ask himself questions about his aides...It is high time to draw the conclusions from this failure, and for everyone to take the consequences," Mazeaud said.
